turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Tell me about the project you really owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, first suspicion, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest bug was duplicate cards. Sometimes one day card showed up twice, but only on slow networks. I first suspected the backend was sending the same event twice. Then I logged every raw event with its id and timestamp on the client. The log showed the events were different, but my reconnect re-read the stream from the start. So the repro was a slow network plus a dropped connection, and the log proved the bug was on my side.
card.then: Next: how I fixed the reconnect so it doesn't replay old cards.

more: The fix was to remember the last event id I had already shown, and on a reconnect I send that id and ask for what comes after it. The server would need to support that, so I confirmed the contract with the backend. I also drop any event whose id I've already seen, as a second guard.

turns.name: W4-concurrency
turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.say: These are two separate intents, each with its own client transfer ID, so they're not duplicates of one transfer. The server handles them one at a time: it locks A's balance row, or runs a conditional update that only debits when the balance is at least 8000 cents, in the same transaction as the credit. The first one succeeds, so A goes from 10000 to 2000 cents and B from 0 to 8000. The second one fails the balance check, so it's rejected and no money moves. Each phone shows only its own result: one success, one clear failure, and both read the balance from the server's record.

card.heard: account switch while A's response is in flight — what goes wrong on Android, how to prevent it
card.say: The old response can land after the switch, so account C could see A's balance or result. I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation. When a response comes back, I drop it if its session is no longer current. The UI only reads the cache for the current account, so C never sees A's data. turns.question: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?

card.problem: Design the entry flow when a payment starts from a group chat: two contacts named Alex, no reliable amount, and the chat stream drops after the user confirms
card.adopted: The chat only suggests a payment; the user picks the recipient and amount on a native confirmation, and the server binds the approval to payer, recipient, amount and expiry.
card.heard: two weeks, first version, who signs off, spike in pending transfers
card.say: With two weeks, the first version is balance, internal transfer, history, the native confirmation step, and the pending and unknown states. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency wait. The product owner signs off on the scope, and the tech lead signs off on the ledger and idempotency contract. Before release I'd test the cases we already covered: lost response plus process kill, a replay of the same ID, two transfers at once, and an account switch. If pending transfers spike, I'd pause new submissions but keep reads and status checks working. The backend owner and I would reconcile the stuck intents, and we'd resume only when the pending count is back to normal.
card.then: Next: how I'd watch that pending count during the rollout.

more: I'd also cap the pending queue per account, so one stuck client can't crowd out everyone else's transfers. And I'd add an alert on the pending count, so we hear about a spike before users do.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: It was used by travelers on the KKday app, in many markets and languages.
Candidate: They were planning trips by hand: working out the budget, searching products one by one, then putting the plan together.
Candidate: The planner took a destination, a budget and a number of days, and gave back a plan they could book.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan: the agent design, the product and order tools, and the core backend.
Candidate: It ended at the Android side of showing the plan, which I wrote with the app team.
Candidate: Product decisions and the final launch call were not mine.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the SSE stream.
Candidate: When a check failed, the backend retried with the exact error, then fell back to a safe default.
Interviewer: On the KKday trip planner, you said you wrote the Android code that reads the SSE stream — what else on the Android side did you build yourself, and what did the app team own?
Candidate: On Android, I also wrote the day-by-day trip cards and the product cards, and the map points.
Candidate: I wrote the SSE reader myself, and the code that shows each card as it arrives.
Candidate: The app team owned the screens around it: the entry point, the loading and empty states, and the final UI polish.
Candidate: So I built the streaming and the card display, and they owned the rest of the page.
Candidate: The fallback only triggers after the checks fail, so a slow stream that never errors still needs its own timeout.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself is the SSE reader.
Candidate: The user enters a destination, a budget and the days, then taps plan.
Candidate: The ViewModel starts the request and collects the stream on a background dispatcher.
Candidate: Each event is parsed into a day card or a product card, and I push it to a StateFlow.
Candidate: The screen collects that state and adds each card as it arrives.
Candidate: If the stream fails halfway, some cards are already on screen, so I show an error banner and keep those days instead of clearing them.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest bug was duplicate cards.
Candidate: Sometimes one day card showed up twice, but only on slow networks.
Candidate: I first suspected the backend was sending the same event twice.
Candidate: Then I logged every raw event with its id and timestamp on the client.
Candidate: The log showed the events were different, but my reconnect re-read the stream from the start.
Candidate: So the repro was a slow network plus a dropped connection, and the log proved the bug was on my side.
Candidate: The fix was to remember the last event id I had already shown, and on a reconnect I send that id and ask for what comes after it.
Candidate: The server would need to support that, so I confirmed the contract with the backend.
Candidate: I also drop any event whose id I've already seen, as a second guard.
Interviewer: You said the log proved the bug was on your side — how did you confirm that the server actually supports the last-event-id resume, rather than just trusting the contract?
Candidate: Right, I didn't just trust the contract.
Candidate: I tested it.
Candidate: I turned the network off in the middle of a stream, then turned it back on.
Candidate: The log showed the reconnect sent the last event id, and the server sent only the events after it.
Candidate: No duplicate cards appeared.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: One was to reconnect and read the stream from the start again.
Candidate: The other was to ask the backend to send the whole plan again on every reconnect.
Candidate: I didn't pick them because both send cards the user has already seen.
Candidate: That means more data and more chances for duplicates.
Candidate: The last event id was the smallest change, and the server already kept the events.
Candidate: The last event id was the smallest change, and the server already kept the events.
Candidate: After release, I checked the logs for reconnects and duplicate cards.
Candidate: I also went through the flow myself on a slow network.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At Debon Securities, I was moving part of our trading app to the new navigation.
Candidate: It was planned for that week's release.
Candidate: During testing I found some old pages had a broken back button.
Candidate: I hadn't checked every page yet, but it could already affect the release.
Candidate: So I told the project manager that same day.
Candidate: I gave him two options: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and test the rest after.
Candidate: He decided to keep the old pages.
Candidate: Everything else shipped on time.

Interviewer: On the Debon Securities release where you kept the old pages, what risk were you willing to accept, who watched the data afterwards, and what signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: The risk I accepted was that some old pages I hadn't checked yet might also have the broken back button.
Candidate: I kept the old pages in that release, so users stayed on the version we already knew.
Candidate: The project manager made the call, and I kept checking the rest and fixed the back button myself.
Candidate: After the release, QA and I watched the crash reports in Bugly, and I watched the feedback from users.
Candidate: The signal to pause would be a jump in crashes on those pages, or users reporting the back button.
Candidate: Then I'd ask for a quick way to turn the new navigation off, and we'd fix it before turning it back on.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Good morning.
Candidate: Before I design, a few questions.
Candidate: Is the balance held by us, or does money move on a bank or card rail?
Candidate: Which currencies do we support?
Candidate: What should work offline?
Candidate: Does that match what you have in mind?

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and what each one owns.
Candidate: The client owns the screens and a local copy of the balance and history.
Candidate: The server owns the ledger, and it's the only place a balance really changes.
Candidate: Local storage is just a cache, so it never decides a transfer.

[board] flowchart TD | A[Client: screens, ViewModel, local cache] -->|send transfer with client ID| B[Server: ledger, one transaction] | B -->|transfer status and new balances| A | B --> C[(Server database: accounts, transfers)] | A --> D[(Local storage: cached balance and history)]
Candidate: The server rejects a duplicate client transfer ID and returns the original result instead of moving the money twice.
Candidate: The client saves the transfer intent with its ID before sending, so a lost response is an unknown outcome, not a failure.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: I'll draw the happy path first, then the lost-response case.
Candidate: A sends 8000 cents with a client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server checks A's balance, then debits A and credits B in one transaction.
Candidate: It returns the transfer status and both new balances, and the app shows success only from that record.

[board] sequenceDiagram | participant A as A app | participant S as Server | participant DB as Ledger DB | participant B as B app | A->>S: send 8000 cents, clientTransferId | S->>DB: begin transaction | DB->>DB: debit A 8000, credit B 8000 | DB-->>S: committed, A 2000, B 8000 | S-->>A: status success, new balances | S-->>B: incoming transfer, new balance | A->>A: result screen shows success
Candidate: The result screen has four states: success, clear failure, processing, and outcome unknown.
Candidate: A timeout is the unknown one, not a failure.

Interviewer: You said the client saves the transfer intent with its ID before sending — on Android, what exactly gets written to local storage at that moment, and how does the app read it back after a restart?
Candidate: If the same ID comes with different details, the server rejects it, so one ID maps to exactly one transfer.

[board] sequenceDiagram | participant A as A app | participant S as Server | participant DB as Ledger DB | A->>S: resend 8000 cents, same clientTransferId | S->>DB: look up transfer by client ID | DB-->>S: one transfer, status success | S-->>A: original status, A 2000, B 8000
Candidate: The amount is a Long in minor units, so 80 dollars is 8000 cents, and I never store money as a float.
Candidate: The row also keeps a timestamp, so I can show how long it has been pending.
Candidate: If the lookup finds nothing, I don't call it a failure: the request may still be in flight, or the read may lag, so the screen stays on outcome unknown and I check again.
Candidate: One edge case: if the client retries with the same ID but a different amount, the server rejects it as a conflict rather than treating it as a new transfer.

Interviewer: Your sequence diagram goes straight from "S-->>A: status success" to "result screen shows success," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before A reopens the app — what changes in your flow? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: The happy path stays the same.
Candidate: What changes is the start: before sending, the app writes the intent row as pending, with its client transfer ID and 8000 cents.
Candidate: After the kill and reopen, the app reads that pending row and queries the server by account and client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server finds the one transfer and returns its original status, A 2000 and B 8000, so the screen shows success from the server's record, not from a guess.

[board] sequenceDiagram | participant A as A app | participant S as Server | participant DB as Ledger DB | A->>A: insert intent row, pending, clientTransferId, 8000 | A->>S: send 8000 cents, clientTransferId | S->>DB: debit A, credit B, one transaction | DB-->>S: committed, A 2000, B 8000 | Note over A: response lost, process killed | A->>A: restart, read pending intents | A->>S: query by account and clientTransferId | S->>DB: look up transfer by client ID | DB-->>S: one transfer, status success | S-->>A: original status, A 2000, B 8000 | A->>A: update row to success, show success

Interviewer: You said that after a restart the app reads the pending row and queries by client transfer ID — but what if that lookup returns not found because the server hasn't committed yet, so the app keeps showing outcome unknown?
Candidate: Right, a not-found answer doesn't prove the money didn't move.
Candidate: The request may still be in flight, or the read may lag behind the commit.
Candidate: So the row stays pending and the screen stays on outcome unknown.
Candidate: I'd check again with a short backoff, and stop after a few tries and show "still checking" with a manual refresh.
Candidate: I'd only mark it failed when the server says the transfer doesn't exist and enough time has passed.

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: These are two separate intents, each with its own client transfer ID, so they're not duplicates of one transfer.

Candidate: The server handles them one at a time: it locks A's balance row, or runs a conditional update that only debits when the balance is at least 8000 cents, in the same transaction as the credit.
Candidate: The first one succeeds, so A goes from 10000 to 2000 cents and B from 0 to 8000.
Candidate: The second one fails the balance check, so it's rejected and no money moves.
Candidate: Each phone shows only its own result: one success, one clear failure, and both read the balance from the server's record.
Candidate: The second one fails the balance check, so it's rejected and no money moves.
Candidate: Each phone shows only its own result: one success, one clear failure.
Candidate: Both phones read the balance from the server's record, not from a local guess.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: The old response can land after the switch, so account C could see A's balance or result.
Candidate: I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When a response comes back, I drop it if its session is no longer current.
Candidate: The UI only reads the cache for the current account, so C never sees A's data.
Candidate: And A's committed transfer stays on the server, so it comes back from A's own history when A signs in again.

Interviewer: You said every request is tagged with the account and a session generation — now the pilot also starts from a group chat with "pay Alex for last night's dinner," two contacts named Alex, and no reliable amount. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see after they confirm and the chat stream disconnects? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.
Candidate: Two things change.
Candidate: The chat only suggests the payment; it never moves money.
Candidate: The user picks which Alex and the amount on a native confirmation screen, and the server binds that approval to payer, recipient, amount and expiry.
Candidate: So a repeated tool call or retry maps to the original intent's ID, never a second transfer.
Candidate: If the chat stream drops right after the user confirms, the app doesn't guess.

[board] flowchart TD | G[Group chat: pay Alex for dinner] --> S[Chat suggests a payment] | S --> C[Native confirm: pick Alex, enter amount] | C --> I[Save intent with client ID] | I --> P[Payment service: one transfer] | P --> R[Result screen reads status by ID]
Candidate: The app reads the status from the payment service by the intent's client ID.
Candidate: If that read times out, the screen stays on outcome unknown, not failure.
Candidate: The user can leave the chat and come back later; the result screen still shows the real status from the server's record.

Interviewer: You said the server binds the approval to payer, recipient, amount and expiry — so what happens if the recipient changes after confirmation, say the chat later resolves to the other Alex?
Candidate: Right, so the approval is bound to the recipient, not just to the amount.
Candidate: The server rejects it as a conflict, and the user has to confirm again on the native screen with the new recipient.
Candidate: The old intent stays pending or expired, and it never moves money.

Interviewer: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?
Candidate: With two weeks, the first version is balance, internal transfer, history, the native confirmation step, and the pending and unknown states.
Candidate: Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency wait.
Candidate: The product owner signs off on the scope, and the tech lead signs off on the ledger and idempotency contract.
Candidate: Before release I'd test the cases we already covered: lost response plus process kill, a replay of the same ID, two transfers at once, and an account switch.
Candidate: If pending transfers spike, I'd pause new submissions but keep reads and status checks working.
Candidate: The backend owner and I would reconcile the stuck intents, and we'd resume only when the pending count is back to normal.
Candidate: I'd also cap the pending queue per account, so one stuck client can't crowd out everyone else's transfers.
Candidate: And I'd add an alert on the pending count, so we hear about a spike before users do.

Interviewer: You mentioned pausing new submissions and capping the pending queue per account — in that rollout, what would you personally own, who would you need on the team, and at what point would you escalate to me?
Candidate: I'd personally own the Android side: the native confirmation screen, the intent row saved before sending, and the result screen with its four states.
Candidate: I'd also own the client-side checks, like dropping a stale response after an account switch.
Candidate: I'd need the backend owner for the idempotency contract and the ledger transaction.
Candidate: I'd need QA to run the failure cases, and the product owner to agree what "outcome unknown" says to the user.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you when the pending count keeps rising after we pause submissions, or when we can't agree who owns the reconciliation.
Candidate: That's a money risk, not a normal bug.
Interviewer: That's it from me. What questions do you have for me about the team or the role?
Candidate: Yes, a few.
Candidate: First, what would you like the new Android engineer to achieve in the first three months?
Candidate: Second, what's the biggest mobile challenge right now: voice response speed, partial results, or reliable actions?
Candidate: And third, how do Android, backend and ML work together when a feature breaks?
